catalog_citation: McPherson, Laura & Matthew S. Dryer. 2021. The tone system of Poko-Rawo (Skou). Phonological Data & Analysis 3(1): 1-32. doi:10.3765/pda.v3art1.54 (CC BY 3.0; publisher PDF from Cambridge Core).
catalog_locator: p. 10, Section 5.2 '/MH/: M with a floating H', paragraph directly after example (8), and footnote 6 (same page); also p. 8, Section 5.1, paragraph after example (4). File: the copy we hold, PDF page = printed page.
catalog_quote: In disyllabic stems, the second syllable is often produced slightly lower than the first. It is unclear whether this should be viewed as a phonological process of downstep, which could indicate that each syllable carries its own M tone, or whether it is a phonetic effect due to the phrase-final position or to a possible stress distinction, as described in other Skou languages (e.g. Donohue 2003).6 [fn. 6:] We thank an anonymous reviewer for this suggestion. While there is no independent evidence for stress, the process of phrase-final reduction could corroborate the prosodic weakness of the final syllable. [p. 8:] This lexically-specified tone association is reminiscent of a much more widespread system of phonological accent proposed for the Skou language by Donohue (2003), wherein accented syllables determine where the tones are associated. It is possible that this system was also once more widespread for Poko, but with its extensive segmental reduction, stems often lose a syllable that may have once carried contrastive accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Poko-Rawo is a three-level tone language (L, M, H, plus toneless syllables and floating tones). The only primary description does not posit word stress: the authors state there is no independent evidence for stress, mention a 'possible stress distinction' (as reported for other Skou languages by Donohue 2003) only as one candidate explanation for the slight lowering of the second syllable of phrase-final disyllables, and note that phrase-medial apocope of final vowels points to prosodic weakness of the final syllable (i.e., if anything, initial-syllable prominence). No stress placement rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the paper also notes (p. 8) that a lexically specified /MH.∅/ association on a few nouns, mostly kinship terms, is reminiscent of the phonological-accent system Donohue (2003) proposed for Skou proper, and speculates such a system may once have been more widespread in Poko before segmental reduction.
new_statements.domain_note: Observations concern stems in isolation / phrase-final position (full forms) versus phrase-medial reduced forms (final vowel apocope); data from elicitation with one primary male speaker, Didicus Mari, in Vanimo, checked against other speakers.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes 'Poko-Rawo' (authors' short name 'Poko'), the Serra Hills Skou language spoken in the villages of Poko, Onip and (formerly) Rawo; this is Glottolog rawo1244 / ISO rwa (Glottolog lists 'Poko-Rawo' as the name in source for this reference). Data come from speakers in Poko village (the language is no longer spoken in Rawo itself).

sources.note: No Poko-Rawo deposit found; ELDP MDP0038 (the grant credited in McPherson & Dryer 2021) is the Walman documentation deposit (Dryer/Brown). Dryer's Buffalo homepage says he and Lea Brown have documented Poko-Rawo since 2001 but lists no Poko-Rawo publication.

sources.note: Section 2 background on Poko segmental/tonal structure (apocope of final vowels phrase-medially, three tone levels, toneless syllables, floating tones); a full-text search for stress/accent finds no mention of stress or accent for Poko (only bibliography entries on other languages).
No phonology, tone or stress information; references are Ethnologue and a village-coordinates dataset only.
